Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

issues.explanation: The Threat items describe a chronic interpersonal/home-intrusion danger template (monitoring for someone entering the home, planning escape routes, feeling unsafe specifically at night), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster. These items imply fear of human attack rather than disaster-related threat.

Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure could occur after a disaster, but in combination with the highly interpersonal Threat items it reinforces a different trauma narrative than natural disaster. The Memory items are disaster-compatible, but the Threat cluster is not clinically coherent with that trauma context.

The threat items are centered on anticipating intentional human intrusion or attack (planning escape routes, listening for someone entering the home), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster. Heightened alertness to loud sounds could fit disaster trauma, but these two more specific threat beliefs imply a different trauma context.

The appraisal 'The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down' is possible after a disaster, but in this profile it pulls toward a betrayal/response-failure formulation that is not supported elsewhere by the selected threat or memory items. Combined with the intrusion-focused threat items, it weakens coherence with a natural-disaster trauma profile.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat item about listening for someone entering the home implies an interpersonal/intrusion danger theme that is hard to reconcile with a primary trauma type of natural disaster. For a natural-disaster profile, loud sounds and generalized hypervigilance are plausible, but specifically monitoring for a person entering the home suggests a different trauma context.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: The appraisal that institutions failed to protect him is possible after a disaster, but in combination with the home-intrusion threat cue it contributes to a mixed interpersonal-threat profile rather than a coherent natural-disaster formulation. The rest of the profile centers on terror, overwhelm, and disorganized memory, so this item is questionable mainly because it pulls toward a different trauma narrative when paired with the flagged threat item.

vignette:
Mark was forty-five, a military medic who had served two tours and a hurricane. The storm came inland with a sound like a freight train, and for seventy-two hours he worked triage in a flooded field hospital, the roar of wind and water and screaming never ceasing. Now, when he tried to remember, the images came in fragments-a child's face, a colleague's hand slipping from his grip, the weight of a body he carried to higher ground-but he could not order them. The sequence was gone, and each fragment arrived with the same visceral terror he had felt that night, so overwhelming that he would have to stop whatever he was doing, breathing fast, eyes fixed on nothing. In the weeks that followed, Mark's beliefs about the world had shattered. He had always believed that effort and protocol could contain chaos, but the hurricane had shown him otherwise: the universe was indifferent, order was an illusion, and nothing he did mattered. This conviction seeped into everything. He stopped feeling that his work as a medic had purpose; his wife's death three years earlier had already hollowed out his private life, and now even his professional identity felt meaningless. He no longer knew who he was.

The hypervigilance set in slowly. At the base, Mark found himself unable to relax. A door slamming in the corridor made him flinch so hard he dropped his coffee. The sudden crack of a helicopter rotor overhead sent his heart into a sprint. He knew intellectually that he was safe, but his body refused to believe it. This constant watchfulness, the way his neck muscles stayed tight even when he sat alone in his quarters, fed the conviction that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that no place was truly secure. His shattered beliefs hardened into a fixed certainty: safety was a myth. And the more he felt that, the more his memories broke through unannounced, each one arriving without the comfort of a story he could control-just raw fragments that proved he was powerless.

The memories and the appraisals tightened into a loop. When Mark recalled the hurricane, he was flooded not only with terror but with a crushing sense that his life had lost its anchor. He had been a man who saved people; now he couldn't even save the memory of who he was. Each recollection deepened his belief that he had become someone unrecognizable, a stranger inside his own skin. And that belief, in turn, made the memories stay longer, because he no longer had any framework-any belief that effort mattered or that the world made sense-to contain them. The fragments just spun, confused and overwhelming.

To manage, Mark began to avoid. He requested desk duty, trading his medic bag for paperwork, because the base clinic's sudden alarms and the crash of gurneys were too much. He stopped attending the unit's informal gatherings-no more barbecues or card games where someone might shout or drop a tray. His colleagues noticed, and he offered vague excuses. The isolation felt safer, but it also deepened his sense of disconnection. He even stopped visiting his wife's grave, because the stillness there only highlighted how far he was from the man who had once believed he could find peace.

Months passed. The hypervigilance remained, the memories kept coming, and the belief that nothing mattered grew heavier. What finally brought Mark to the VA clinic was not a crisis but a quiet morning when he realized he had not felt a single moment of genuine relaxation-not even in the shower, where water on tile sounded too much like rain on a tarp. He was tired of being afraid of his own life. He was afraid that the person he used to be was dead, and that the world truly was as chaotic and merciless as the hurricane had shown him. But he came anyway, hoping that maybe, if someone listened, he might find a thread of order he could follow back to himself.
